title: Security Posture with Defender for Cloud

questions.sub_skill: Identify security risks by using Defender CSPM
questions.prompt: Your organisation enables Defender CSPM. Two weeks later, attack path analysis shows nothing and cloud security explorer returns resources but no vulnerabilities. Most likely cause?
options: The security graph takes 30 days to populate
The plan was enabled by someone without Subscription Owner, so agentless scanning never started — and without it, attack paths and the explorer do not populate with vulnerabilities
Foundational CSPM must be disabled before Defender CSPM can build the graph
Attack path analysis requires a Defender for Servers Plan 2 subscription
questions.explanation: Agentless scanning requires the Subscription Owner to enable the plan. Someone with lower authorisation can enable it successfully — the scanner simply never turns on, the plan reads as enabled, and empty attack paths look identical to a clean environment.
why_not: Waiting will not help. Without agentless scanning running, the graph never receives the vulnerability data that attack paths are built from.
Foundational CSPM does not need disabling. The missing piece is agentless scanning, which starts only when a Subscription Owner enables the plan.
Attack path analysis is a Defender CSPM capability. The problem is that the plan's agentless scanning never started.
questions.scenario_clue: "attack path analysis shows nothing" and the explorer has "no vulnerabilities" - the agentless scanner never started.
questions.misconception: That a plan showing as enabled means all its components are running.

questions.sub_skill: Identify security risks by using Defender CSPM
questions.prompt: Distinguish a recommendation from an attack path, using one virtual machine as the example.
options: An attack path is a recommendation with a higher severity score
A recommendation is one finding; an attack path is a chain — internet exposure plus a vulnerability plus an identity plus permissions on something sensitive — assembled from the security graph
A recommendation applies to a resource; an attack path applies to a subscription
An attack path is a recommendation that has been open for more than 30 days
questions.explanation: Three separate, individually unremarkable findings become one urgent item when the graph connects them. That assembly is what turns a four-thousand-item list into a priority, and it is the conceptual core of Domain 4.
why_not: An attack path is not one finding with a higher score. It is several findings connected by the security graph.
Scope is not the difference. An attack path runs through specific resources, joining findings that are individually unremarkable.
Age has nothing to do with it. An attack path is assembled from connected findings, however new they are.
questions.scenario_clue: "distinguish" with "one virtual machine" - single findings versus a connected chain.
questions.misconception: That an attack path is just a more severe recommendation.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate compliance against security frameworks by using Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: Your classic secure score in the Azure portal is 82%, and an internet-facing VM with a critical CVE holds a managed identity with Contributor at subscription scope. What is that secure score actually measuring?
options: Risk-weighted exposure across the estate
Compliance against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark — not risk, which is why an unaddressed attack path can coexist with a high score
The proportion of resources covered by workload protection plans
The ratio of resolved to open recommendations
questions.explanation: The classic secure score is computed from built-in Microsoft cloud security benchmark recommendations, and risk prioritisation doesn't affect it. It measures what is assessed, not what is dangerous. The Defender portal's Cloud Secure Score is a separate, risk-based model that weights recommendations by asset risk factors and criticality - but it still scores findings asset by asset; chaining them into an attack path is Defender CSPM's job.
why_not: The classic score isn't risk-weighted: only built-in MCSB recommendations count, and risk prioritisation doesn't affect it. The risk-weighted model is the Cloud Secure Score in the Defender portal.
Plan coverage is not what the score counts. It is computed from MCSB-based controls.
It is not a count of resolved recommendations. It is computed from MCSB-based controls, and it measures what is assessed, not what is dangerous.
questions.scenario_clue: "classic secure score is 82%" alongside an obvious attack path - the classic score measures benchmark compliance, not risk.
questions.misconception: That a high secure score means low risk.

questions.sub_skill: Enable and configure Defender for Cloud workload protection plans
questions.prompt: A workload protection plan must apply to subscriptions your organisation creates next year, not just the ones that exist today. How?
options: Enable the plan at the tenant root management group in Defender for Cloud
Assign the built-in Azure Policy that configures the plan, at management group scope
Enable the plan on each subscription and turn on inheritance
Plans apply to new subscriptions automatically once enabled anywhere
questions.explanation: Plans are enabled at subscription scope and manual enablement covers only what exists. Assigning the policy is the governance pattern from 01-03 applied to workload protection — and note that a policy will re-enable a plan you turn off, so remove the assignment first when tearing down.
why_not: Plans are enabled at subscription scope, and manual enablement covers only subscriptions that exist. Future subscriptions need the policy.
There is no plan inheritance to turn on. Manual enablement covers only the subscriptions that exist today.
Enabling a plan covers the subscription it was enabled on. New subscriptions start without it.
questions.scenario_clue: "subscriptions your organisation creates next year" - only policy at a parent scope reaches resources that do not exist yet.
questions.misconception: That enabling a plan once covers future subscriptions.

questions.sub_skill: Connect hybrid cloud and multicloud environments to Defender for Cloud, including Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)
questions.prompt: You create an AWS security connector but decline Azure Arc auto-provisioning for the discovered EC2 instances. What do you lose?
options: Nothing — the connector covers all capabilities natively

Agent-based Defender for Servers protection on those machines: without Arc, Defender for Cloud cannot deploy the Defender for Endpoint and vulnerability assessment extensions to them, although agentless scanning still assesses them
The ability to see them in the same secure score
Cross-cloud attack paths, which require Arc on both sides
questions.explanation: The connector establishes read access, discovers resources and applies the equivalent assessments, and with Defender for Servers Plan 2 or Defender CSPM, agentless scanning still reads the machines' disks. Arc is what gives each machine an Azure resource ID and an extension host, so Defender for Cloud can deploy Defender for Endpoint and the vulnerability assessment extension, and Azure Policy and Machine Configuration can reach it.
why_not: The connector gives read access, discovery and assessments - plus agentless scanning with the right plan - but Defender for Cloud cannot deploy the Defender for Endpoint extension to a machine that is not Arc-enabled.
The connector's assessments still reach Defender for Cloud. What you lose is agent-based server protection on the machines.
What Arc adds is an Azure resource ID and extension host for each machine, which Defender for Endpoint deployment, Azure Policy and Machine Configuration need. That is the loss here.
questions.scenario_clue: "decline Azure Arc auto-provisioning" - the machines get no Azure resource identity, so Defender for Cloud cannot deploy extensions to them; only agentless coverage remains.
questions.misconception: That a cloud connector alone gives full server protection.

questions.sub_skill: Configure Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management settings for Azure VMs
questions.prompt: A requirement says vulnerability findings for Azure VMs must be produced without installing anything on the machines. Which configuration satisfies it?
options: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management via the Defender for Endpoint extension
Agentless scanning through disk snapshots, available with Defender for Servers Plan 2 or Defender CSPM
Azure Machine Configuration with a guest assignment
Network Watcher connection troubleshoot
questions.explanation: MDVM reaches Azure VMs two ways: with the Defender for Endpoint extension, which is an agent, and agentlessly through disk snapshot scanning. Only the second satisfies 'without installing anything', and its findings feed the security graph.
why_not: The Defender for Endpoint extension is an agent, so it fails 'without installing anything'.
Machine Configuration needs its own extension on the VM, and it assesses configuration, not vulnerabilities.
Connection troubleshoot tests network reachability. It produces no vulnerability findings.
questions.scenario_clue: "without installing anything on the machines" - agentless snapshot scanning.
questions.misconception: That vulnerability assessment always needs an agent.

questions.sub_skill: Discover unprotected assets and vulnerabilities by using Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management (EASM)
questions.prompt: Your internal inventory is complete and your secure score is 90%. What class of asset does Defender EASM find that neither can?
options: Resources in subscriptions you do not own
Internet-facing assets nobody in the organisation remembers owning — a marketing microsite, a forgotten test environment, a subsidiary's infrastructure
Assets missing a workload protection plan
Machines whose agents have stopped reporting
questions.explanation: EASM works outward from seeds - domains, IP blocks, hosts, ASNs, WHOIS organisations - and builds an inventory of what an attacker sees. That is shadow IT, the category most likely to be unpatched, unmonitored and unowned. Billing counts assets in the Approved Inventory state, and discovery approves strongly connected assets automatically, so seed narrowly.
why_not: EASM does not look inside Azure subscriptions at all. It works outward from seeds such as domains and IP blocks to find what an attacker can see.
A missing workload protection plan shows up in Defender for Cloud itself. EASM finds assets that are not in your inventory at all.
Machines whose agents have gone quiet are still in your inventory. EASM finds internet-facing assets that never were.
questions.scenario_clue: "internal inventory is complete" - EASM looks from outside, at what you did not know to inventory.
questions.misconception: That a complete internal inventory covers everything internet-facing.

questions.sub_skill: Evaluate compliance against security frameworks by using Defender for Cloud
questions.prompt: An auditor needs your Azure subscriptions assessed against PCI DSS in the Defender for Cloud Regulatory compliance dashboard. The only paid plan enabled today is Defender for Servers Plan 1. What must change before you can add the standard?
options: Nothing - Foundational CSPM includes every regulatory standard
Enable a Defender plan that unlocks compliance standards - for example Defender CSPM - because Defender for Servers Plan 1 alone does not
Assign the PCI DSS initiative in Azure Policy; the dashboard is not involved
Connect the subscription to Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager first
questions.explanation: MCSB is applied for free. Additional standards need a paid Defender plan - Microsoft documents any plan except Defender for Servers Plan 1 or Defender for APIs Plan 1. Defender CSPM is the usual choice. Adding the standard then needs Owner or Policy Contributor.
why_not: Foundational CSPM gives you MCSB and the secure score, not additional regulatory standards.
Standards are Azure Policy initiatives, but the requirement is to assess in the Defender for Cloud dashboard, which needs a qualifying plan to show added standards.
Compliance data flows from Defender for Cloud to Compliance Manager, not the other way round, and it is not a prerequisite for adding a standard.
questions.scenario_clue: "only paid plan enabled today is Defender for Servers Plan 1" - one of the two plans that does not unlock compliance standards.
questions.misconception: That any Defender plan, or the free tier, unlocks additional compliance standards.
